content: The World Health Organization (WHO) panel recommends the use of a combination therapy of liposomal amphotericin B (L-AMB) and miltefosine over L-AMB monotherapy for individuals with visceral leishmaniasis (VL) and HIV co-infection in South-East Asia. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low-certainty evidence. The suggested regimen includes L-AMB administered up to a total dose of 30 mg/kg (5 mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11) combined with miltefosine at 100 mg/day for 14 days. For L-AMB monotherapy, the total dose is up to 40 mg/kg (5 mg/kg on days 1–4, 8, 10, 17, and 24). Patients diagnosed with VL should have their HIV status determined, and routine screening for tuberculosis (TB) should be conducted at the time of VL diagnosis, with follow-up evaluations. For patients who do not show a good clinical response, therapy may be extended for an additional course after ruling out other diagnoses. If miltefosine is unavailable or contraindicated, L-AMB monotherapy (up to 40 mg/kg) can be considered. Comprehensive clinical management is essential, including adequate HIV treatment and nutritional support. Women of childbearing potential should have access to contraception and pregnancy testing before receiving miltefosine. The WHO panel also recommends secondary prophylaxis after the first episode of VL in HIV-VL co-infected patients in East Africa. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-certainty evidence. Pentamidine isethionate (4 mg/kg per day, or 300 mg for adults, every 3–4 weeks) is recommended in East Africa, while amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg every 3–4 weeks) or L-AMB (3–5 mg/kg every 3–4 weeks) is suggested in South-East Asia. Prophylaxis can be discontinued if the CD4 cell count is maintained above 350 cells/mm³ or if the HIV viral load is undetectable for at least six months, with no evidence of VL relapse. When selecting a drug for secondary prophylaxis, it is important to avoid using the same drug that was used to treat the primary VL episode. The choice should also consider the safety profile, potential collateral benefits (e.g., prevention of other infections), and the risk of drug resistance. Strengthening health infrastructure, human resource capacity, and coordination among HIV, VL, and related programs (e.g., TB and vector control) is also critical. Monitoring and evaluation should include indicators such as the proportion of VL cases screened for HIV, the proportion of HIV-positive VL cases treated, relapse rates, and patient survival at six and 12 months. Research priorities include better understanding the epidemiology and progression of VL in HIV patients, developing simpler therapeutic and prophylactic regimens, and improving safety data for long-term miltefosine use. Operational research is needed to explore systematic screening strategies in high HIV-VL prevalence areas and to integrate VL and HIV programs effectively.
